title: How every scam is built, and the two-minute check that stops it

say: How every scam is built, and the two-minute check that stops it.
This is the video for module one of Scam Awareness and Digital Trust: how scams work and how to spot them.
A pickpocket takes your purse. A scammer makes you open the purse yourself and give it away, often while saying thank you.

panel.heading: A scammer makes you open your own purse
items: You hand over money, codes or details yourself
The bank sees a payment you authorised
So recovery is slow, sometimes impossible
The best protection is a habit in your head

say: Because you made the transfer, typed the PIN or shared the code, the bank's records show a payment you authorised.

say: New scams appear every month. But underneath, they are built from the same three parts. Spot the parts, and you do not need to memorise every trick.
First, the story. A believable reason to act.

panel.heading: Every scam needs these three parts

cards.d: A believable reason to act: your BVN will be blocked, you won a promo, your son is in trouble.
Act now, before you think or ask anyone. Do it in 10 minutes. Don't tell anyone.
Always the same few things: money, a code such as your PIN or OTP, or your personal details.

say: Second, the pressure. You must act now, before you think, and often keep it secret so nobody can warn you.

panel.heading: Every scam needs these three parts

cards.d: A believable reason to act: your BVN will be blocked, you won a promo, your son is in trouble.

Always the same few things: money, a code such as your PIN or OTP, or your personal details.

say: Third, the request. It is always money, a code, or your personal details.
A real offer survives you slowing down and checking. A scam cannot. That is why pressure is always in the package.

say: She never entered a promo. She calls her network on the official number from her SIM pack, not a number in the SMS. There is no promo. She deletes it, and warns her women's group.

say: Scams work on feelings, not on lack of intelligence. Doctors, bankers and pastors have lost money too. Fear is the first lever.

panel.heading: Six feelings scammers use
items: Fear: your account will be blocked today
Greed or hope: double your money in 30 days
Urgency: offer closes in 15 minutes
Authority: this is EFCC, or your bank
Love and trust, or shame and secrecy

say: Halima, a teacher in Kaduna, got a call. He knew her name and her bank. Someone is withdrawing 180,000 naira right now, he said. Read me the code we just sent.
Authority, fear and urgency together. She noticed her fear.

panel.heading: The cool-down rule saved Halima
items: Notice the feeling and name it
End the call: I will call the bank myself
Check through a number you found yourself
Tell one trusted person before paying

say: She said, I will call the bank myself, and hung up.

say: She called the number on the back of her ATM card. Nobody from the bank had called. The code was for a transfer the scammer was trying to make.

say: Because she did not read it out, the transfer failed. Remember, a caller who knows your name and account number is not proven genuine. Account numbers are shared every day to receive payments.

panel.rule: Strong feeling plus money or codes: stop for at least 10 minutes.

say: Ask these five questions of any message, call or offer. One red flag is enough to stop.
A request for your PIN, password, OTP or card details is always a scam, because no genuine bank or office needs them from you.

panel.heading: The two-minute check
items: Asks for a code or PIN?
Pay before you receive?
Rushing or secrecy?
Unofficial channel or link?
Too good to be true?

say: Amaka runs a provision shop in Onitsha. A customer bought goods worth 38,500 naira, showed a transfer successful screen, and an SMS credit alert arrived. He was in a rush.

panel.heading: SMS alert or real balance?
right: Your balance in your bank app
A shop rule on a card by the till

say: She opened her bank app. Her balance had not changed. She said, I will release the goods once it shows in my app. He left without them. A screenshot is a picture, not money.

panel.heading: SMS alert or real balance?
right: Your balance in your bank app
A shop rule on a card by the till

say: To remember. Every scam has a story, a pressure and a request. Pause, verify through your own channel, talk to someone you trust, and report.
Never share a code. Trust your balance, not an SMS. And fraud is a crime, so reporting is nothing to be ashamed of.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Every scam: a story, pressure and a request
Real offers survive checking; scams need you to rush
Pause, verify, talk, report
Never share your PIN, password or OTP
Trust your app balance, not an SMS or screenshot
